What the original study did not say

The Yerkes-Dodson law was not about stress

The famous inverted U of performance comes from an experiment with mice and shocks.

It is common to see an inverted-U curve: with little arousal we perform poorly, with moderate arousal we perform best and with too much our performance drops. It is called the Yerkes-Dodson law.

The original experiment

In 1908, Robert Yerkes and John Dodson trained mice to choose between a white box and a black one, giving them a shock when they chose wrongly. They varied the strength of the shock and the difficulty of the task. They found that for difficult tasks a moderate shock sped up learning more than a strong one. They did not measure arousal or stress.

The interpretation as a link between arousal and performance came decades later. As a general idea it is still useful, but it is more a rule of thumb than a precise law: the relationship varies with the person, the task and the type of stress.

References

  1. Yerkes, R. M. y Dodson, J. D. (1908). The relation of strength of stimulus to rapidity of habit-formation. Journal of Comparative Neurology and Psychology, 18(5), 459–482.
  2. Teigen, K. H. (1994). Yerkes-Dodson: A law for all seasons. Theory & Psychology, 4(4), 525–547.
